newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy ERM entry faces tough rate choice - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Italy ERM entry faces tough rate choice - analysts.

text.p: Italy is determined to stick to its own timetable for entry to Europe's currency grid, despite the Finnish markka's early link, but the main sticking point is likely to be the lira's entry rate, analysts said on Monday.

Finland's markka joined Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) on Saturday, leaving just Italy, Sweden, Greece and Britain outside. Although Italy is clear favourite to join next, the Italian government is in no immediate hurry.

"The Italian government has said that the budget needs to be approved before ERM entry, and then there is the key question over the entry rate," said Francesco Giordano, senior economist at Italy's San Paolo bank.

Italy's prime minister Romano Prodi has stressed that the nation's key 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) deficit-cutting 1997 budget needs to be approved by parliament before ERM talks can get seriously underway.

This budget measure needs to be passed by the year-end, but it seems set for a stormy passage through parliament with the centre-right opposition scenting that the budget is too heavy on extra taxes and too light on spending cuts.
Italy's government is determined to re-enter the ERM as an obvious precursor to being among the first batch of European nations entering a European single currency in 1999.
Two years of membership of the ERM is necessary for European Monetary Union (EMU), and Italy is keen to get in as quickly as possible to show its determination to be ready for EMU in 1999.

"Once the budget process is out of the way, clearly the government's number one priority is ERM entry. But with the lira having depreciated as much as 40 percent from its 1992 level, entry rate is a key issue," said international economist Ken Wattret at investment bank Paribas in London.

In recent weeks, the lira has appreciated strongly as Italy unveiled its tough 1997 budget and showed its determination to meet EMU criteria. The Italian currency is currently trading around 994 lire to the German mark, but still well short of its old ERM levels.

The lira tumbled out of the ERM in September 1992 along with Britain's pound. Its central rate had been fixed at 748.217 lire per mark, then was devalued by seven percent mid-month, but then suspended all ERM obligations three days later.

Economists pointed out that French President Jacques Chirac, seeing French industry hurt by cheap Italian imports after the lira's ERM exit, wants a strong lira of around 950 lire to the mark, but Italian industrialists mindful of Italy's slowing exports want a weaker value of around 1,050 lire, compared with 995 at 1245 GMT.
Giorgio Radaelli, economist at Lehman Brothers sees a "huge gulf" between these two views, and any agreement on an exchange level will be difficult to reach on this key issue.
Paribas's Wattret sees a 1,000 lire a mark compromise entry level, with France having to soften its stance to allow Italy into the ERM at a rate which can be sustained.
The Bank of Italy will probably want to stick to informal fluctuation bands of six percent within formal 15 percent bands, and it will need a level that it can defend, he suggests.

San Paolo's Giordano sees France wanting a lira ERM entry at 925-950 lire while the Italian government is looking for 1,025-1,050 lire, but even a 1,000 lire level could be hard for Italy to swallow given weak export growth and orders as the lira has firmed strongly in recent weeks, he adds. ($1=1,522 lire)
